items.title: How to Transition Your Hair Routine From Summer to Fall, by Hair Type
items.summary: August is when your hair can start noticing fall before you do. Summer asks your hair to navigate heat, humidity, UV exposure, sweat, and frequent styling. As the season changes, cooler temperatures and lower humidity change the environment around the hair fiber, too. By September and October, a routine designed primarily to manage summer humidity may no longer be addressing what your hair needs most. But that doesn't mean you need an entirely new routine. It means understanding how your hair structure responds to its environment and adjusting where your routine puts its focus. Because hair isn't random. Its behavior is largely determined by its structure, and that structure responds to moisture, friction, heat, humidity, and the condition of the cuticle. Why the Summer-to-Fall Transition Matters for Your Hair The outer layer of your hair, the cuticle, acts as a protective barrier. Along with the hair's natural lipid layer, it helps regulate how moisture moves into and out of the fiber. When that surface system is intact, hair is better able to resist excess water. When it becomes compromised by heat, chemical processing, friction, or environmental stress, moisture movement becomes less controlled. That's when you may notice roughness, dryness, frizz, or a loss of definition. Humidity adds another layer to the equation. Inside the cortex, hydrogen bonds are temporary connections that help maintain the shape of the hair. Water can break and reform these bonds, which is why humidity can change how hair behaves. When moisture enters the fiber unevenly, the hair can swell and shift shape, creating the frizz and flyaways associated with humid weather. As the air becomes drier, the problem can change. Instead of primarily managing excess moisture coming from the environment, your routine increasingly needs to help retain moisture within the hair. Dry air also makes static more noticeable because electrical charges don't dissipate as easily. Friction from sweaters, hats, scarves, pillowcases, and brushing can make those flyaways even more obvious. That doesn't mean every hair type needs the same amount of moisture. In fact, this is where hair type matters most. Straight Hair: Keep Cleansing Balanced, Add Lightweight Protection Straight hair has a relatively uniform fiber structure, so sebum can travel easily from the scalp toward the ends. That's one reason straight hair can become oily or look weighed down faster than other hair types. At the same time, over-washing can contribute to dryness, particularly through the lengths and ends. As fall approaches, the goal isn't to suddenly stop cleansing. It's to balance cleansing with moisture retention. Continue focusing shampoo on the scalp, where oil and buildup accumulate, while keeping heavier conditioning products away from the roots. Depending on scalp activity, straight hair may need cleansing every one to three days. Then add lightweight protection to the lengths. A leave-in treatment on damp hair can provide light moisture and help reduce flyaways without overwhelming the strand. For a finishing step, a lightweight serum can smooth the surface, add shine, and provide a protective layer against dryness and static. Your fall focus: hydration without weight, balanced cleansing, and protection for dry ends. Try: Custom Straight Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Straight Hair Mask once a week, Straight Hair Leave-In, and Custom Hair Serum. Wavy Hair: Move From Humidity Control to Moisture Balance Wavy hair sits in the middle of the spectrum. Its S-shaped pattern creates bends along the fiber, which means sebum doesn't travel as evenly as it does along straight hair. The result can be familiar: oily roots, dry ends, and a wave pattern that seems to have a mind of its own. In summer, humidity can disrupt those waves by changing the temporary bonds inside the cortex. In fall, lower humidity can shift the problem toward dryness, static, and loss of definition. The answer isn't simply adding the heaviest product you can find. Wavy hair benefits from balanced moisture that supports the wave without stretching it out. Keep cleansing gentle and focus shampoo on the scalp. On days when your hair doesn't need a full wash, refreshing with conditioner or a lightweight leave-in can help maintain moisture without repeatedly cleansing the strand. As the air gets drier, your mask can also become more important. The Wavy Hair Mask with vegan squalane provides deeper conditioning for waves that are feeling dry or more prone to frizz. For styling, apply your wave-defining product to soaking-wet or damp hair and scrunch rather than brushing through afterward. That helps preserve the natural wave pattern instead of breaking it apart. Your fall focus: balanced moisture, wave definition, and less friction. Try: Custom Wavy Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Wavy Hair Leave-In Treatment, Wavy Hair Mask one to two times a week as needed, and Zero-Gravity Styling Mousse for definition. Curly Hair: Prioritize Moisture Retention, Not Just Hydration Curly hair has a structural challenge that doesn't disappear when summer ends: the bends and curves in the fiber make it harder for natural oils to travel from the scalp to the ends. That's why curly hair can feel dry even when the scalp doesn't. The shape of the fiber also means the cuticle is less uniformly aligned, which can make moisture move in and out more readily. Dryness isn't a sign that your hair is doing something wrong. It's geometry. Fall makes moisture retention even more important. Rather than simply adding more water-based hydration, think about what happens after hydration. A leave-in treatment helps maintain moisture throughout the day, while a curl cream conditions the surface of the strand and helps support definition. Layering products allows you to build the amount of moisture and control your individual curls need. As fall progresses, make deep conditioning a consistent part of your routine. The Curly Hair Mask, formulated with coconut oil and shea butter, provides more intensive conditioning for curls that are feeling dry or less defined. And keep friction low. Avoid dry brushing, detangle while conditioning, and consider a silk or satin pillowcase to reduce friction and moisture loss while you sleep. Your fall focus: moisture retention, definition, low friction, and consistent conditioning. Try: Custom Curly Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Curly Hair Mask, Curly Leave-In Treatment, and Super Shape Curl Cream. Coily Hair: Protect the Moisture You've Worked to Keep Coily hair has the most complex pathway for natural oils to travel. Tight bends and turns create more points of friction and stress along the strand, while the cuticle is more separated and less uniformly aligned. That makes coily hair particularly susceptible to moisture loss, dryness, and breakage. Again, this isn't a flaw. It's the physics of the fiber. When humidity drops, moisture retention becomes even more important. For coily hair, the goal should be less about repeatedly adding moisture and more about keeping that moisture in the fiber. Gentle cleansing helps preserve the hair's surface lipids, while rich conditioning and leave-in products provide ongoing support. Coily hair generally benefits from less frequent cleansing—often every five to seven days depending on scalp needs and lifestyle—with shampoo concentrated primarily on the scalp. After conditioning, layer your leave-in while the hair is still wet, followed by your styling product. For additional protection, a serum can provide another surface layer that helps reduce moisture loss, friction, and static. As fall moves toward winter, protective styling and low-manipulation routines become increasingly useful for minimizing mechanical stress. Your fall focus: moisture retention, lipid support, low manipulation, and protection from friction. Try: Coily Hair Shampoo + Conditioner, Coily Hair Mask, Coily Leave-In Treatment, and Custom Hair Serum. One Important Note About Porosity You may have heard that straight hair is low porosity and curly or coily hair is high porosity. There's some structural reasoning behind those tendencies, but hair type and porosity aren't the same thing. Porosity describes how easily hair absorbs and retains moisture, and it's influenced by the condition of the cuticle. Damage from chemical processing, heat, friction, and environmental stress can change how porous hair behaves. Two people with the same curl pattern can therefore have very different moisture needs. That's why your routine should respond to both your hair type and your hair's current condition. If your waves suddenly feel dry, your curls aren't holding, or your straight hair feels rough at the ends, don't assume you need an entirely different routine. Look at what your hair is telling you about moisture retention, surface condition, buildup, and friction. The Fall Hair Rule: Follow the Structure The biggest seasonal shift isn't about replacing your entire summer routine. It's about changing what your routine is designed to do. In summer, your hair may need more support against humidity, heat, UV exposure, and environmental moisture. In fall, lower humidity and increasing friction can make moisture retention, conditioning, and static management more important. And the right adjustment depends on your hair's structure. Straight: Keep it light. Balance cleansing with hydration and protect the ends. Wavy: Keep the balance. Add conditioning without sacrificing your wave pattern. Curly: Layer moisture and focus on retaining it. Coily: Prioritize moisture sealing, low manipulation, and protection. Your hair doesn't need to follow the calendar perfectly. It just needs a routine that understands how its structure responds when the environment changes. Because great hair care isn't about fighting your hair. It's about understanding it.

items.title: Silicone in Hair Care: Separating the Myths from the Science
items.summary: Silicone has become one of the most misunderstood ingredients in hair care. Today, "silicone-free" appears on countless product labels, often alongside claims like "sulfate-free" and "paraben-free." But unlike a trend, hair biology doesn't change. For years, silicones have been praised for delivering slip and shine… and criticized for causing buildup and dullness. So which is it? The truth is, silicone isn't inherently good or bad for your hair. Its performance depends on the type of silicone, the formula it's used in, and most importantly, your hair type. At Function of Beauty, we believe understanding how ingredients work is more valuable than avoiding them based on a label. Here's what silicone actually does and when it can be beneficial. What Does Silicone Do for Hair? Every strand of hair is protected by a layer called the cuticle. Think of it as your hair's outer shield. It controls how moisture moves in and out of the strand, influences shine, and plays a major role in how smooth—or frizzy—your hair feels. Silicones form a lightweight film over the cuticle that helps support its natural function. Depending on the formula, they can: Smooth the cuticle to reduce friction between strands Minimize frizz and static Increase shine by creating a smoother surface that reflects light Help protect hair from heat styling Slow excess moisture movement that contributes to frizz in humid conditions These benefits aren't just cosmetic—they're rooted in how hair behaves. When humidity rises, water moves into the hair unevenly, causing the strand to swell and disrupting its shape. That's what creates frizz. By helping regulate moisture movement across the cuticle, silicones can improve smoothness and definition while reducing unwanted expansion. Why Silicone Gets a Bad Reputation Not all silicones behave the same way. Some traditional silicones, like dimethicone, are less water-soluble and can build up over time if they're used repeatedly without an effective cleansing routine. That buildup—not the silicone itself—is what can leave hair feeling heavy, coated, or dull. Many newer silicone technologies work differently. Lightweight silicones, including ingredients like amodimethicone, cyclomethicone, and dimethiconol, are designed to provide conditioning, shine, and heat protection while rinsing away more easily within a typical shampoo routine. The conversation around silicone became especially prominent through curly hair routines like the Curly Girl Method, which often minimize or eliminate silicones, which specifically uses co-washing (no shampoo) as the primary cleansing step. In that routine, non-water-soluble silicones genuinely accumulate, because there's nothing in the wash cycle capable of removing them. The advice to avoid heavy silicones made perfect sense within that context. In those routines, avoiding heavier silicones makes sense because they're not regularly being removed. Over time, that advice expanded beyond its original context, turning "silicone-free" into a universal marketing message. In reality, the best choice depends entirely on your hair type, styling habits, and how often you use a clarifying shampoo. Here’s where things get interesting. Many products labeled “silicone-free” replace silicones with waxes or heavy oils, which can also form barriers and create dulling, hydration-blocking buildup if not properly removed. In other words, a product with a “silicone-free” callout does not automatically guarantee the healthiest results! How Silicone Works for Different Hair Types Hair type influences how hair reacts to moisture, heat, and styling products. Your hair type shapes your daily care routine and styling choices. Porosity, thickness, and texture greatly influence how silicones behave. Straight Hair Straight hair typically has a flatter, tighter cuticle that naturally allows oils to travel easily from scalp to ends. Because of that, heavier silicones can sometimes leave hair feeling weighed down more quickly. Lightweight silicone-containing products, however, can still be incredibly beneficial. Heat protectants and lightweight styling products can help reduce static, add shine, and protect against thermal damage without sacrificing movement. Wavy Hair Wavy hair often sits between straight and curly hair in both structure and moisture needs. It tends to be more susceptible to frizz because the cuticle isn't perfectly uniform along the wave pattern. Lightweight silicones can help smooth the cuticle, support wave definition, and reduce humidity-induced frizz while maintaining softness and bounce. Curly Hair Curly hair naturally loses moisture more easily because the cuticle is more lifted and the curl pattern makes it harder for natural scalp oils to travel down the strand. For curls, silicone can help lock in hydration after moisturizing products have been applied, reduce tangling, improve slip, and create longer-lasting curl definition. The key is choosing formulas that balance moisture with effective cleansing. Coily Hair Coily hair has the greatest need for moisture retention and experiences the highest amount of friction during detangling and protective styling. Silicone can help reduce breakage by improving slip, minimizing friction between strands, and helping seal moisture into the hair. Regular cleansing remains important, but avoiding silicone altogether isn't necessary for many coily hair routines. Should You Avoid Silicone? The better question isn't "Is this silicone-free?" It's: Which silicone is being used? Does this formula match my hair type? Does my wash routine remove buildup when needed? Hair care works best when every product in your routine works together. If you're using heavier styling products, an occasional clarifying shampoo or a double cleanse can help remove buildup. If you're using lightweight conditioning silicones as part of a balanced routine, they may provide exactly the smoothness, shine, and frizz control your hair needs. The Bottom Line Hair care isn't about avoiding ingredients; it's about understanding them. Silicone remains one of the most effective ingredients available for improving shine, reducing friction, protecting against heat, and helping manage frizz. Whether it's the right choice depends on your hair's structure, your styling habits, and your overall routine. At Function of Beauty, we believe the best routine starts with your hair type and not with marketing claims. Because when you understand how your hair works, choosing the right products becomes a whole lot easier.

items.title: How Summer Changes Your Hair: A Hair Type Guide to Restoring Moisture and Shine
items.summary: By late July, your hair has weathered weeks of sun, humidity, chlorine, salt water, and heat styling. The frizz, flatness, dryness, or breakage you're noticing isn't random—it's a reflection of what's happened to your hair's structure over time. Every strand responds differently based on its hair type, but the science is the same: summer gradually changes how your hair holds moisture, protects itself, and behaves. Here's what's happening beneath the surface, and what an effective late-summer reset actually looks like. Why Summer Is Structurally Demanding on Hair Hair behaves the way it does because of how it's built: a cortex (the inner protein structure that provides strength and elasticity), a cuticle (the overlapping outer layer that protects the strand), and a lipid layer that coats the surface and regulates moisture movement. Summer challenges all three parts of the hair structure. UV rays gradually break down proteins in the cortex while oxidizing the protective lipids on the surface. Chlorine strips away that lipid layer, leaving the cuticle rougher and more vulnerable to moisture loss. Humidity repeatedly forces water into and out of the hair, temporarily disrupting hydrogen bonds inside the cortex and causing the cuticle to lift, leading to frizz and loss of shape. Over weeks of sun, swimming, heat, and humidity, these effects compound. The result isn't damaged hair overnight—it's hair that feels drier, rougher, less defined, and harder to manage because its natural protective structure has been worn down. A late-summer reset isn't about reversing every day at the beach. It's about restoring moisture, smoothing the cuticle, and reinforcing your hair's natural barrier so it can perform the way it was designed to. Straight Hair: Buildup Is Your Main Issue Straight hair's round follicles create a smooth pathway for sebum to travel from the scalp to the ends. That efficient oil distribution keeps strands naturally conditioned, but in summer it also means sweat, sunscreen residue, and styling products become noticeable more quickly. As oil and environmental buildup spread across the hair shaft, straight hair can look flat, heavy, or greasy sooner than other hair types. The result: By late July, flat roots and dull mid-lengths usually aren't about dryness. They're about buildup sitting on a cuticle that's been lying flat the whole time. Your reset: Start with a thorough shampoo wash focused on the scalp — the Straight Hair Shampoo is formulated with coconut water to remove buildup without stripping the lightweight moisture balance straight hair needs. Follow with Straight Hair Conditioner (avocado oil, applied mid-lengths to ends only), and swap in the Straight Hair Mask once this week for a deeper treatment. The seaweed extract supports cuticle alignment, which is what gives straight hair its reflective quality when it's performing well. Wavy Hair: You're Fighting Two Things at Once Wavy hair's oval follicle creates its characteristic S-shaped pattern, making it harder for sebum to travel evenly from roots to ends. During summer, sweat, sunscreen, and styling products can build up more quickly at the roots, while the mid-lengths and ends receive less natural conditioning. The result: UV exposure gradually degrades the hair's protective lipid layer, and humidity repeatedly lifts the cuticle as moisture moves in and out of the strand. The result is hair that's oily at the roots, drier through the lengths, and more prone to frizz. Your reset: The Wavy Hair Shampoo handles the scalp without over-drying stressed ends. Use Wavy Hair Conditioner from mid-lengths down only. Mid-week, try a Co-Wash application instead of a second shampoo — it hydrates your lengths without adding to scalp buildup. Finish the week with the Wavy Hair Mask (vegan squalane) in place of conditioner for 10 minutes. For styling, scrunch Zero-Gravity Styling Mousse into soaking wet hair and let it air dry without touching. Curly Hair: Moisture Loss Is Structural, and Summer Makes It Worse Curly hair's spiral structure makes it difficult for sebum to travel from the scalp to the ends, leaving the mid-lengths and ends naturally drier than straighter hair types. During summer, UV exposure gradually weakens the hair's protective lipid layer, while humidity repeatedly swells and contracts the cuticle as moisture moves in and out of the strand. Over time, these stressors make curls less efficient at retaining moisture. The result: curls that once had defined, springy shape may become frizzier at the crown, drier through the lengths, and less responsive to the products and routines that usually work. Your Reset: Shampoo once this week — over-cleansing strips the little natural oil curly hair does produce. Use Curly Hair Conditioner generously, working through with fingers while wet. Mid-week, swap in the Curly Hair Mask for 10 minutes (mango butter and coconut oil work at a level a rinse-out conditioner can't match). Layer Curly Leave-In Treatment over damp hair before styling, then scrunch Super Shape Curl Cream for definition and frizz control. Coily Hair: Your Structure Needs Intentional Replenishment Coily hair has the most tightly coiled structure of any hair type, making it the most challenging for sebum to travel from the scalp to the ends. As a result, coily hair is naturally drier and relies more heavily on its protective lipid layer and external moisture to maintain softness and flexibility. During summer, UV exposure gradually degrades those surface lipids, while humidity causes repeated swelling and lifting of the cuticle, making it even harder for the hair to retain moisture. The result: hair may feel drier, rougher, and more fragile, with less stretch, more shrinkage, and increased breakage if moisture isn't consistently replenished. Your reset: Use the Custom Co-Wash to cleanse the scalp while delivering moisture to the lengths simultaneously. Follow with Coily Hair Conditioner, then seal with Coily Leave-In Treatment while hair is still soaking wet. Use the Coily Hair Mask twice this week in place of conditioner — murumuru butter nourishes deeply and reduces the surface friction that drives roughness. For coily hair specifically, the Custom Hair Serum (available through our quiz) is a worthwhile add as a final sealing step after your leave-in on days when your structure needs that extra moisture lock. The One Thing All Hair Types Have in Common Right Now Every hair type responds to summer the same way: the cuticle has been cycling through moisture and heat repeatedly for weeks, and it needs consistency. A single deep conditioning treatment won't undo two months of summer, but a reset week with the right products for your specific structure gets your hair behaving the way it did before summer. Your structure already knows what it needs. Now you do too.

items.title: How to Get a Salon Worthy Blowout at Home
items.summary: A great blowout isn't just about technique. It's about working with your hair type, protecting your hair from heat, and creating a routine that builds smoothness, volume, and shine from the start. Whether your hair is straight, wavy, curly, or coily, understanding how heat changes your hair's structure can help you achieve longer-lasting results with less damage. Drying your hair in sections creates smoother, longer-lasting results. Allowing each section to cool helps lock in shape and volume. Lightweight styling products help support movement, reduce frizz, and improve longevity without weighing hair down. Why Hair Prep Matters Your blowout starts long before you pick up a blow dryer. Healthy-looking blowouts begin with hair that's clean, hydrated, and conditioned for your hair type. Step 2: Rough Dry First Instead of immediately reaching for a round brush, begin by rough drying your hair until it's about 70-80% dry. Step 3: Choose the Right Tools Your technique matters, but so do your tools. Always use a concentrator nozzle on your blow dryer. Medium round brush: Adds body with soft bends. Paddle brush: Creates a sleek, smooth finish. Step 4: Work in Sections Divide your hair into manageable sections before styling. Working with smaller sections allows heat to reach each piece evenly while maintaining the tension needed for a smooth finish. Place your brush underneath each section and slowly pull through while following closely with your dryer. Keep the airflow moving from roots to ends to encourage the cuticle to lie flat. Continue until each section is completely dry before moving to the next. Step 5: Let Your Hair Cool Heat temporarily reshapes the hydrogen bonds inside your hair, but cooling is what helps set your style. After drying each section, leave it wrapped around the brush or pin it loosely for several seconds before releasing. This simple step helps improve volume, bounce, and longevity. Step 6: Finish Your Style Once your hair has completely cooled, finish with a few drops of Custom Hair Serum through the mid-lengths and ends for added shine and frizz control. If you want additional volume, gently lift your roots with your fingertips instead of adding more heat. Add Styling Primer to help minimize humidity-related frizz and hold your style. Coily Hair Begin with well-conditioned hair and use smaller sections with consistent tension. Add Styling Primer to help minimize humidity-related frizz and hold your style. The Bottom Line A salon-worthy blowout isn't about using the highest heat or the most products. It's about understanding how your hair responds to moisture, heat, and styling. When you start with products personalized to your hair type and goals, protect your hair during styling, and use the right technique, you can create a smooth, voluminous blowout that lasts longer while helping keep your hair healthy over time.

items.title: Sweat, Sunscreen, and Scalp Buildup: A Hair Type Guide to Summer Scalp Care
items.summary: Summer doesn't just change how your hair looks and feels. It changes what's happening at the scalp. Sweat, sunscreen, extra time outdoors, and shifting wash schedules all affect your scalp first. How your scalp responds depends entirely on your hair type. The Science Behind Summer Scalp Care Every hair type has a different relationship with sebum, the natural oil your scalp produces. The shape of your hair fiber determines how easily that oil travels from root to end. During summer, heat, sweat, and sunscreen residue all interact with that process differently. Understanding your hair's structure is the difference between guessing at a routine and building one that works with your scalp instead. How to Remove Sunscreen, Sweat, and Build-up Sunscreen formulas are water-resistant and contain zinc oxide or waxes, so you may need to apply your hair type shampoo directly to your roots and let it sit for 2 to 3 minutes to thoroughly break down the residue. If you are still feeling like you have residue on your hair, repeat the shampoo and double cleanse. Double cleansing means shampooing your hair twice during the same wash. The first cleanse lifts away sweat, excess oil, sunscreen, and product buildup from the scalp. The second cleanse gives your scalp a deeper clean, allowing your shampoo to work more effectively and leaving your hair feeling fresher and more balanced. First Cleanse: Thoroughly wet your hair, then work a quarter-sized amount of shampoo between your palms before applying it to your scalp. Using your fingertips, gently massage for 30 to 60 seconds to loosen buildup and impurities. Rinse thoroughly. Second Cleanse: Apply a slightly smaller amount of shampoo to your scalp. Because the initial buildup has already been removed, you'll notice a richer lather. Continue massaging your scalp, allowing the lather to glide through the lengths of your hair as you rinse. Finish by rinsing until the water runs clear. Straight Hair: Managing Faster Oil Production Straight hair's flat, tightly aligned cuticle allows sebum to travel from root to tip with the least resistance of any hair type. That's one reason straight hair often looks naturally shiny. During summer, however, heat and increased perspiration can accelerate oil buildup, leaving the scalp feeling greasy sooner than usual. items.title: Why Does Hair Frizz in Summer? Hair Care Tips for Every Hair Type
items.summary: Humidity season is here, and if your hair has its own opinion about the weather, you're not imagining it. Frizz isn't a flaw — it's physics. And once you understand what's actually happening at the strand level, you can stop fighting your hair type and start working with it. Frizz Is Structural, Not Random Here is the science: Hair is made primarily of keratin, a strong structural protein that naturally absorbs and releases water. On humid days, keratin draws moisture from the air into the hair shaft. As the hair absorbs that extra water, it swells, temporarily changing the hydrogen bonds that help determine your hair's shape. If moisture enters unevenly, the cuticle can lift, leading to frizz, puffiness, or a loss of definition. How much this happens depends on your hair's structure, which is why straight, wavy, curly, and coily hair each respond differently to humidity. That's also why a one-size-fits-all anti-frizz product rarely works for everyone in the room. Straight hair, wavy hair, curly hair, and coily hair each let moisture in and let it out differently, which means each one needs a different defense. As hair type experts, this is the exact problem we built Function of Beauty around: structure-matched care, not guesswork. How Frizz Shows Up by Hair Type Straight hair lies closest to the scalp, so it tends to pick up humidity fast and go flat or limp rather than visibly frizzy, though flyaways are still frizz's cousin. Straight hair's sebum (its natural oil) distributes easily down the shaft, which is great for shine but means it can look greasy before it looks frizzy. Wavy hair sits between straight and curly. It has more volume than straight hair but less natural definition than curly hair, which makes it prone to both frizz and a kind of directionless puff when humidity hits. Curly hair has a curled hair shaft that affects how oil travels from root to tip. That uneven oil distribution is why curls can look dry and frizzy at the same time. It can be one or the other, or both, for a structural reason. Coily hair has the tightest curl pattern and the most cuticle separation, making it both the most porous and the most fragile hair type. Sebum can't really navigate those tight coils. This leaves the hair chronically dry. When dry, the outer layer (cuticle) lifts, allowing humidity from the air to enter the shaft, causing the strands to swell and expand Matching Your Hair Routine to Your Hair Structure This is why we created our Hair Type Collections. Every shampoo and conditioner, leave-in treatment, and mask is formulated with the unique characteristics of straight, wavy, curly, and coily hair in mind, helping each hair type respond better to humidity with the moisture, lightweight care, or nourishment it needs. Curly Hair Shampoo & Conditioner, with flaxseed extract and Brazilian pracaxi oil, hydrate while gently cleansing, which helps curls stay defined instead of fighting both dryness and frizz at once. Coily Hair Shampoo & Conditioner, with chia seeds and Jamaican black castor oil, deliver the intensive moisture coily hair needs from root to tip, since it can't rely on its own sebum to do that work. If you're curly or coily, this is also a great season to lean on our Co-Wash. It's gentler than a full shampoo and lighter than a conditioner, so it won't strip the moisture your curls are working hard to hold onto. We recommend alternating it with your shampoo to keep your scalp clean without over-drying your strands. Twice a week, for any hair type dealing with humidity-related dryness, our Hair Mask gives you a deeper dose of conditioning with ingredients like shea butter, jojoba ester, and argan oil that go to work for 5 to 10 minutes to help reinforce the cuticle layer that humidity loves to disrupt. The Last Line of Defense: Sealing It All In Once your cleanse-and-condition routine is structure-matched, the final step is locking that moisture in before it has a chance to escape or before outside humidity has a chance to get in. For most hair types, that means a styling product that seals the cuticle rather than just sitting on top of it. If you've got a specific frizz-prone day ahead of you — a wedding, a humid vacation, a big presentation and want something built around your exact hair goals, our Custom Hair Serum is formulated to reduce frizz by 70% and protect against thermal damage up to 400°F, with your choice of hair goals layered in. It's a nice option to have in your back pocket for the days your regular routine needs backup. The Takeaway Frizz isn't a sign your hair care routine is failing; it's your hair's structure responding to its environment exactly the way it's built to. The fix isn't more product; it's the right product for your specific hair type. That's the whole idea behind Function of Beauty: we don't guess at what your hair needs. items.title: Pool, Sun, and Salt Water: A Hair Type Expert's Guide to Summer Hair Survival
items.summary: Chlorine, salt water, and UV exposure can change the way your hair looks, feels, and behaves. The reason isn't random, and it affects every hair type. The way your hair responds to pool water, ocean water, and sun exposure depends on its hair type, cuticle structure, moisture retention patterns, and daily routine. Understanding those differences can help you build a routine that works with your hair instead of against it. Hair damage occurs when the protective, outer layer of your hair, also known as the cuticle, is compromised, leaving cracks in its exterior. Once cracked, the cuticle lifts, resulting in dull, dry, frizzy, or brittle hair. It can be a nightmare, but all hope is not lost! While you may not be able to completely repair hair that is already damaged, there are still plenty of steps you can take to help prevent it from happening in the future. Building Your Hair Type's Summer Defense The good news is that protecting your hair during the summer doesn't require a complicated routine. We created a bundle just for you: Summer Rescue Bundle. This 3-step smoothing system is designed to help improve the feel of rough, dry, and hard-to-manage hair. Formulated with hydrating ingredients, this system helps support hydration at the cuticle level, restoring softness, strengthening hair, improving manageability, and making hair feel smoother. A few simple steps before and after swimming can help support moisture retention, improve manageability, and reduce the effects of repeated environmental exposure What Chlorine, Salt Water, and Sun Actually Do to Hair Hair is made primarily of protein called keratin and protected by an outer layer called the cuticle. The cuticle acts as the hair's first line of defense, helping regulate moisture retention and protecting the inner structure of the fiber. Chlorine weakens keratin, which is the structural protein that gives hair its elasticity, resulting in split ends and breakage. Exposure to saltwater and UV rays physically pulls moisture from your strands through osmosis, leaving them dehydrated. Salt acts as a sponge, pulling water out of the hair shaft, which gives it a parched, straw-like texture. When this happens, moisture can escape more easily, the hair surface may become rougher, and strands can appear drier, duller, or more prone to frizz. Color-treated hair may also experience faster fading when exposed to the sun and pool water. Using the right products can help reduce breakage and recover from the summer stressors that we put on our hair. The goal is to understand how your hair's structure responds to summer conditions and support it accordingly. Sun, Salt Water, and Chlorine Affect Every Hair Type Differently Hair type isn't just how your hair looks. It's how it functions. The shape of the hair fiber influences how oils travel, how moisture is retained, and how the hair responds to environmental stressors like chlorine, UV exposure, humidity, and salt water. Straight hair shows structural damage quickly through frizz, limpness, and a straw-like texture, but it also weighs down easily if you use products that are too heavy. Avoid rubbing your hair with heavy beach towels, which roughs up the hair cuticle and causes extreme frizz. Instead, gently blot your hair or wrap it in a soft microfiber towel or cotton t-shirt. Wavy Hair Wavy hair (Type 2) sits between straight and curly hair in terms of moisture distribution. The bends in the hair strand make it slightly harder for oils to travel evenly, which can make waves more susceptible to frizz and moisture loss during the summer months. Sun exposure, chlorine, and humidity can disrupt wave definition, leaving hair looking less uniform and more prone to expansion. For wavy hair, protecting your pattern means balancing heavy moisture retention with curl-safe detangling. Wavy hair is naturally more porous and prone to frizz than straight hair, meaning chlorine and salt water can completely flatten your wave definition and turn your texture coarse or stringy. Curly Hair Curly hair (Type 3) naturally experiences greater challenges with moisture distribution because oils must travel around multiple curves and bends in the hair fiber. Protecting your curls from chlorine and saltwater is all about maximizing moisture barriers and preventing severe shrinkage and matting. Curly hair (Type 3) is naturally highly porous, meaning it absorbs damaging pool chemicals and salt like a sponge, leading to extreme frizz and hair damage. Coily Hair Coily hair (Type 4) has the most complex strand geometry of all hair types, making moisture retention especially important. Because natural oils have the hardest time traveling from root to end, coily hair often relies heavily on conditioning and moisture-focused routines to maintain softness and manageability. After swimming or prolonged sun exposure, coily hair may experience increased dryness and require additional hydration to help support the cuticle and maintain moisture balance. 4-Step Pre-swim Prep Routine before stepping into the water: Saturate with fresh water: Soak your hair completely under a tap or beach shower. Hair acts like a sponge; filling it with clean water prevents it from absorbing chemical pool water or drying salt water. Apply a leave-in conditioner: Coat your damp strands from roots to tips to create a water-resistant barrier. Use a leave-in conditioner built for your hair type. Put hair in a protective style: Secure your hair to minimize water friction, tangles, and matting. Use a high bun for straight hair, loose braids for wavy hair, and tight twists for curly hair. Wear a silicone swim cap: For the ultimate protection, tuck your prepped hair inside a silicone swim cap. This physically blocks the majority of the water from ever touching your strands. The best summer routine isn't about fighting your hair. It's about supporting the way your hair naturally functions so it can better withstand everything summer throws at it. Post-swim Routine for Your Hair Type (Straight, Curly, Coily, Wavy) Straight Hair: Focus on Cleansing With Lightweight Moisture Straight hair typically distributes natural oils more efficiently from root to end, which helps support shine and smoothness. After repeated swims and frequent washing, however, that natural lubrication can be reduced, leaving hair looking duller or feeling dry at the ends. Delivers up to 24 hours of humidity and frizz control without leaving a crunchy texture.Color & UV Defense: Formulated with rice seed protein to defend hair color from fading and protect strands from sun-induced UV damage. Wavy Hair: Focus on Moisture Balance and Definition Wavy hair sits in the middle of the moisture spectrum. It can become oily at the roots while still experiencing dryness through the mid-lengths and ends. Summer conditions often amplify frizz and make waves lose their natural definition. After swimming, use the Wavy Hair Shampoo to gently cleanse away chlorine and saltwater residue. Curly Hair: Focus on Moisture Retention and Curl Definition Curly hair naturally experiences greater challenges with moisture distribution because oils must travel around bends and curves throughout the strand. When chlorine, salt water, and sun exposure enter the equation, curls may feel drier, less defined, and more prone to tangling. Between wash days, use the Custom Co-Wash to gently cleanse the scalp and hair without removing the moisture your coils need to stay manageable. Formulated with Jamaican black castor seed oil and avocado oil, this co-wash moisturizes and protects coily, curly, and color-treated hair. Our Curly Hair Super Shape Curl Cream defines and hydrates curls with a flexible, touchable hold that never feels crunchy or sticky. items.title: Splitting Hairs: How to Treat 4 Types of Split Ends
items.summary: If you ask any hair stylist about the most common hair complaint they hear from clients, there’s a good chance it’s split ends. The annoying feather-effect they have on the ends of hair strands is anything but glamorous. Split ends can make hair look overwhelmed with frizz, dryness, and damage — definitely not words to describe healthy hair. While it might sound like we’re splitting hairs here, the truth is that there are different types of split ends. Each type indicates a different level and severity of hair damage. Luckily, there are ways to prevent, reduce, and alleviate split ends. Here’s what you need to know. The 4 Types of Split Ends As much as we don’t like to admit it, there's something kind of fascinating about split ends. Sure, they’re annoying and unsightly, but at the same time, examining the nitty-gritty details of a split end is like looking at your blackheads in a magnifying mirror. You hate that they're there yet you can't look away. Since we know you're curious about what can cause split ends and how you can get rid of them, let's investigate the four common types of split ends. Then, you can then begin to address the issues behind them. 1. Y-Split This is the prototypical split end. It looks like a "Y" where two separate sections have each split about 1/4" or more from each other. Y-split ends indicate the beginning stages of hair splitting, and are generally a sign of mild hair damage. Fortunately, you can give these types of split ends a softer look and feel with proper hydration. Pro Tip: Follow these 16 tips on how to moisturize hair 2. Feathered A hair strand with feathered split ends will look like a tree branch that has a bunch of twigs attached to it. Each split will vary in length, up to half an inch. Feathered split ends are an indicator of severely damaged hair. If you find a lot of feathered splits in your hair, this is a sign that your hair cuticles need some serious TLC. Pro Tip: Get a primer on hair cuticles to help tame your split ends 3. Candle This type of split end looks like a candlestick with a lit flame. The candlestick part of the hair shaft is as thick as the rest of the hair strands while the flame part appears to be about half the width of that. This is because the tip of the hair strand has been eroded, making it look like an entire layer of the cuticle has been peeled away. When this type of split end is grown out, it can make the strands weaker and thinner. Pro Tip: Check out these hacks for making thin hair look thicker 4. Single-Strand Knots This type of split end looks like a piece of rope that’s tied in a knot. Single-strand knots are usually caused by aggressive treatment of hair and are more common for those with coily or curly hair types. When a knot is formed in the hair, it makes detangling much harder. Oftentimes, when a brush or comb is run through dry hair, breakage occurs. Pro Tip: Learn how to avoid curly hair mistakes What Do Split Ends Say About Your Hair? No matter what kind of split ends you have, they’re all indicators that you have some degree of hair damage that needs to be addressed. Here’s what you need to know about haircare habits that might be causing your ends to split and what approach you can take to free yourself from split end stress. Your Heat Setting Are Too High You don't need to be a cosmetologist to know that heat styling tools can lead to frizzy hair, damage, and yes, split ends. But did you know that the duration, temperature, and proximity at which you style your hair is what affects your strands the most? In a study on hair shaft damage from hair dryers, different groups were tested to see how air drying affected their hair versus blow drying. For the blow-drying group, it was found that the longer and hotter the hair was treated, the more splitting occurred. However, those who used a continuous motion and held the blow dryer six inches away from their head tended to have less hair splitting and breakage than naturally dried hair. So what does this say? It says that hot tools can lead to split ends. But it also shows that using them on a consistent basis and at high temperatures is the real culprit. If you want to continue using blow-dryers and straighteners, do so with caution. Limit usage to once or twice a month and use products with heat protectant properties, such as Function of Beauty's custom hair serum. This lightweight serum can be used on damp or wet hair to help increase shine, smoothness and hydration. It's also been shown to: Reduce frizz by 70% Improve detangling by 75% Thermally protect hair up to 400 degrees You Need a Haircut No matter what types of split ends you have, these damaging dead ends have no place in your hair. Letting them stick around can wreak major havoc on your locks. The more stress and friction you enforce on your split ends, the more likely they’ll spread damage and splittage to the mid-length sections of your hair. To put an end to this, you need to get regular trims. It's simple but true. The best way to get rid of split ends is to cut them off at the source. As soon as your see splits start to form, head to the salon and snip away. If you catch them in the early stage of development, you'll probably only have to trim off a quarter-inch or so. This option is much better than having to cut off multiple inches because you've let your damage run the ends of your hair ragged. Regular trims are especially helpful if your dreams of growing long hair are being cut short by nasty split ends. Pro Tip: Learn how a haircut can change your hair for the better Too Much Shampooing, Not Enough Conditioning Washing your hair with shampoo too often can cause abrasion to the surface of your hair. However, conditioning can help protect the surface of your hair fibers and prevent damage from destructive grooming and chemical treatment habits. Plus, the protein-derived substances used in conditioners can help temporarily reduce the look of split ends. Since conditioning is such an important factor in protecting your hair from damage, consider adding a leave-in conditioner to your hair care routine. You can use it post-shower or apply it to dry hair to help smooth out the frizzy look that split ends can create. Function of Beauty's custom leave-in treatment gives split end-prone hair a much needed dose of shine and hydration thanks to naturally derived and synthetic ingredients like avocado oil, argan oil, and coffee extract. It’s Time to Get a Handle on Your Split Ends Having a few (or even a lot) of split ends doesn't mean you're doomed to a life of flyaways and frizz. It just means that you need to change up your hair habits and find the right hair products to help mask them. Using lower temperatures when heat styling, adding a leave-in conditioner to your haircare routine, and trimming your split ends as soon as they pop up will help you keep your split ends in check and prevent future ones from popping up. To protect your hair color, control oiliness, define curls, and address split ends all at once, take our custom hair quiz. Here, you can design a custom hair care formulated for your unique hair type and hair goals.

items.title: Sweet Almond Oil for Hair: Don't Miss Out on These 4 Benefits
items.summary: When it comes to adding hair oils to your hair care routine, you may want to give sweet almond oil a try. Sure, coconut oil gets lots of love for its nourishing and moisturizing capabilities. But its rich oily texture is best reserved for drier and coarse hair types. Meanwhile, sweet almond oil is lighter in texture without compromising on hydration. That's why it's a universally appealing oil for all hair types. But what are the exact benefits of sweet almond oil for hair? And how can you use it to make your mane gloriously luscious? Read on for the answers to your most-asked questions. Sweet Almond Oil for Hair: Back to Its Roots Did you know there are two types of almond oils: sweet almond oil and bitter almond oil? Due to sweet almond oil's beauty benefits, it's often found in skincare and haircare products, which is why it's the star of this article. Sweet almond oil is extracted from the kernels of ripened sweet almonds. The almond tree (Prunus dulcis) is native to Asia and the Middle East, and its fruits were documented as early as 780,000 B.C.E. Today, America is the largest almond producer in the world, specifically the state of California. In terms of hair care, the the profile of sweet almond oil is pretty impressive as it's infused with: Omega fatty acids, like oleic acid, linoleic acid, and palmitic acid Vitamin E, which is a fat-soluble antioxidant Essential minerals, including potassium, phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium Polyphenols, which have antioxidant properties You should also know that cold-pressed sweet almond oil is considered unrefined, as it retains more of its beneficial nutrients. On the other hand, refined sweet almond oil usually undergoes some form of heat and/or chemical processing to extend its shelf life. 4 Benefits of Sweet Almond Oil for Hair OK, you are now an expert on the various nutrients sweet almond oil possesses. But how do they relate to the health of your hair? Mainly, in the following four ways. 1. An Incredible Softener for Rough Strands Because sweet almond oil is an incredible emollient at heart, it's the go-to softener for hair. ICYDK what emollients are, they are hydrating oils that fill in the gaps of your hair cuticles (the outermost protective layer of your hair shaft) to keep moisture in. Your cuticles have overlapping, scale-like cells to maintain optimal hydration levels, and the cuticles also protect the inner parts of the fiber (read: the cortex and the medulla). Healthy cuticles mean that every scale lies perfectly flat with little to no "pores" (aka low porosity hair). Unfortunately, external stressors like heat, chemicals, and friction raise the cuticle layer and create more pores than you would like. As a result, the uneven cuticles of high porosity hair lead to a roughened texture. This is where sweet almond oil helps your strands. Using its emollient superpowers, it fills in the pores for a smoother cuticle and seals in moisture. Well-moisturized strands thus feel softer to the touch. 2. A Miracle Oil for Dull-Looking Hair The cuticle-smoothing ability of sweet almond oil also works wonders to create glossy-looking hair. That's because flatter, smoother cuticles do a better job of reflecting light and the oil creates a glossy film on your fibers to supercharge their natural radiance. As you can imagine, this two-way approach makes your hair shinier than ever. 3. A Formidable Tamer for Frizz and Flyaways One of the major benefits of almond oil is that it helps tone down unwanted frizz and flyaways. But first, let's look behind the scenes to understand why your hair turns frizzy. When your hair cuticles are peppered with pores, your mane loses more moisture than it retains. This leads to insufficient lipids in your hair shafts (think ceramides, cholesterol, and fatty acids). Unfortunately, these internal hair lipids cannot be replenished through your scalp's natural oils. In an attempt to compensate for the increased dryness, your fibers absorb the surrounding water droplets in the air. This causes your hair shafts to swell and frizz. So, how can you restore the internal moisture levels of your fibers without the dreaded frizz? The answer: sweet almond oil. As we've mentioned, sweet almond oil contains omega-3 fatty acids, which is part of your fibers' natural lipid profile. Applying the oil to your tresses helps restock your inner hair oils sans the frizz. Aside from using sweet almond oil straight from the bottle as a natural moisturizer for dry hair and dry scalp, look for hair products that contain it as an ingredient. For example, you can add the "volumize" hair goal to your Function of Beauty custom shampoo and conditioner. 4. A Friction-Reducing Balm for Hair Breakage We all know that combs and tangled hair don't mix well — can you say unwanted breakage and split ends? But sweet almond oil can help eliminate the struggle of knots and snarls. One study involving Brazilian oils and butters found that the botanically derived oils: Increased the ease of combing wet hair Significantly enhanced hair gloss Reduced the risk of split ends In other words, applying sweet almond oil (also a plant-based oil) to your strands makes hair brushing a breeze, and puts you closer to achieving that healthy hair look. How to Use Sweet Almond Oil for Hair Just like other lightweight carrier oils — think jojoba and olive oils — you can use sweet almond oil on its own or mixed with essential oils. How to use sweet almond oil on its own: Rub a few drops of sweet almond oil between your palms to warm up the oil. Apply the oil to your hair with your hands in a praying motion from the mid-length down. If you're struggling with dry skin on your scalp, apply the oil from roots to tips. Gently brush through your mane with a wide tooth comb to minimize breakage and ensure every strand is evenly coated with the oil. This is a good time to work out the kinks. Leave the oil on for at least 30 minutes before shampooing. If you have an oily scalp, start with only 1-2 drops of sweet almond oil and concentrate it on the ends of your hair. This way, you can let the oil hydrate your locks without risking too much product buildup. How to use sweet almond oil as a DIY hair mask: Peel and remove the pit of one ripe avocado, then mash it thoroughly Combine coconut oil and sweet almond oil in a mixing bowl in a 2:1 ratio Add the mashed avocado to the bowl and mix well Apply the mixture to damp hair from the roots to the tips Let the mask sit for 30 minutes before rinsing it off with water Follow up with your usual shampoo and conditioner routine Because sweet almond oil is such an easy haircare ingredient to play with, you can easily mix and match with other hair-healthy ingredients. For example, you can swap out avocado and coconut oil for lightweight ingredients like honey and yogurt. Reap the Fruits of Sweet Almond Oil for Hair Sweet almond oil for hair is one of the best ways to treat your tresses. After all, who doesn't want to get rid of too-rough strands, dullness, frizz, and split ends? You can go the DIY route (which we've listed above) or choose hair products infused with sweet almond oil — the latter is great if you simply want convenience. To see sweet almond oil on the ingredient list of your haircare products, choose the "volumize" hair goal when you take our hair quiz. It's time to reap the fruits of sweet almond oil for hair.

items.title: Winter Hair Care Tips: How to Prevent Dry Hair, Static, and Breakage
items.summary: Winter changes how your hair behaves. Nothing about winter hair behavior is random. Its structure responds to its environment. If your hair feels drier, frizzier, or more prone to static during winter, nothing is "wrong" with it. It's simply responding to its environment. Hair fibers naturally exchange moisture with the air around them. During winter, cold air holds less moisture, and indoor heating further reduces humidity levels. In low-humidity environments, dry air seeks moisture equilibrium and naturally draws water out from the inner hair fiber (the cortex). This moisture loss causes the protective outer layer (the cuticle) to lift. As the hair fiber dehydrates, the outer cuticle layer becomes rigid, raised, and rough, leading directly to dullness, static, frizz, and breakage. The good news? A few strategic adjustments can help support your hair's structure and keep it performing at its best all season long. Why Does Hair Get Dry in Winter? Dryness is not random. It is structural. Your hair's cuticle acts as a protective barrier that controls moisture exchange between the hair fiber and the environment. During winter, low humidity, indoor heating, and temperature fluctuations can cause moisture to leave the hair more quickly than it can be replenished. As moisture levels decrease, the cuticle becomes rougher and less effective at retaining hydration. This can lead to: Dryness Frizz Static Dullness Increased breakage Protecting moisture retention becomes one of the most important goals of a winter hair care routine. 1. Protect Hair From Cold Weather Hats, scarves, and hoods don't just keep you warm. They help shield your hair from cold air, wind, and moisture loss. Satin-lined or silk-lined hats are the best way to prevent damage and lock in moisture. The smooth surface prevents friction and eliminates static 2. Never Go Outside With Wet Hair Wet hair is more vulnerable to stress because the hair fiber swells when it absorbs water. When hair is swollen, the internal bonds that help maintain its structure become easier to stretch and disrupt. Combined with cold temperatures, this can increase the likelihood of breakage and roughness. Allow your hair to dry completely before heading outdoors whenever possible. 3. Fight Winter Static by Supporting Moisture Balance Static is not a flaw. It's physics acting on dry fiber. When humidity levels drop, electrical charges build more easily on the hair shaft. Friction from hats, scarves, sweaters, and brushes transfers electrons to the hair, causing strands to repel one another and creating flyaways and static. For straight and wavy hair, a personalized Leave-In Conditioner can help replenish moisture while smoothing the cuticle. Following with a Custom Hair Serum helps create a lightweight barrier that seals in hydration, reduces friction, and minimizes static buildup throughout the day. For curly and coily hair, Function of Beauty Super Shape Curl Cream for Curly Hair can provide additional moisture retention and cuticle support while helping curls stay defined and aligned in dry winter conditions. 4. Wash With Lukewarm Water Hot showers feel great in winter, but excessive heat can accelerate moisture loss from the hair fiber. Washing with lukewarm water helps cleanse the hair while preserving more of the moisture needed for softness, flexibility, and shine. Cooler rinses may also help support a smoother cuticle surface, which can improve light reflection and overall shine. 5. Use a Humidifier Indoors Indoor heating systems dramatically reduce moisture levels in the air. A humidifier helps restore humidity to your environment, reducing the amount of moisture drawn from your hair and skin throughout the day. Think of it as supporting your hair before you even step into the shower. 6. Switch to a Microfiber Towel Traditional bath towels can create friction that roughens the cuticle and increases breakage. Instead, gently blot excess water using a microfiber towel or soft cotton T-shirt. Less friction helps maintain a smoother cuticle and reduces unnecessary stress on the hair fiber. 7. Extend Time Between Washes Natural oils help lubricate the hair shaft and support moisture retention. Because winter conditions can already leave hair feeling drier, extending time between wash days may help preserve some of the scalp's natural protective oils. If your hair and scalp tolerate it, consider washing less frequently during colder months. 8. Deep Condition Weekly When winter air pulls moisture from the hair fiber, restoring hydration becomes essential. A weekly Hair Mask helps support moisture retention by conditioning the cuticle and improving the hair's ability to hold onto hydration. This is especially important for curly, coily, color-treated, or high-porosity hair, which naturally loses moisture more quickly. Consistent deep conditioning can help improve softness, manageability, and resilience throughout the season. 9. Reduce Heat Styling and Use a Heat Protectant Hair that is already experiencing seasonal moisture loss may be more vulnerable to heat-related stress. Heat styling repeatedly disrupts hydrogen bonds inside the hair fiber and can contribute to cuticle wear over time. Function of Beauty recommends using a styling primer formulated with provitamin B5 that provides color, UV, and heat protection (up to 450°F). Formulated for your unique hair goals with a personalized level of hold. Whenever possible, embrace your natural texture or reduce styling temperatures. If heat styling is part of your routine, apply a personalized Styling Primer beforehand to help support the hair fiber and reduce thermal stress during styling. 10. Personalize Your Routine for Your Hair Type Every hair type responds differently to winter. Straight hair often benefits from lightweight hydration and moisture retention without added weight. Wavy hair typically needs balanced moisture and frizz management. Curly hair benefits from increased moisture support because natural oils have a harder time traveling through bends and curves in the hair shaft. Coily hair often requires deeper hydration and moisture retention because its structure creates more opportunities for moisture loss along the fiber. Because every hair type has a different architecture, the most effective winter routine is one designed around your unique hair structure and behavior. Shop your hair type HERE. The Bottom Line Winter hair challenges are the result of changing humidity, moisture movement, and environmental stressors. Focusing on moisture retention, minimizing friction, supporting the cuticle, and protecting the internal structure of the hair fiber can help you reduce dryness, static, and breakage throughout the season. Foods rich in biotin include: Eggs, salmon, avocados, sweet potatoes, sunflower seeds, almonds, beef liver. 4. Foods rich in folate include: Lentils, chickpeas, black beans, spinach, asparagus, Brussels sprouts, and avocados. 5. Vitamin C Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress. It also supports collagen production, a structural protein found throughout the body. Vitamin D Vitamin D plays a role in many bodily functions, including supporting healthy skin and scalp health. items.title: 6 Hair Color Ideas to Compliment You

Concerned about compromising the health of your hair? We’re also here to offer tips on maintaining your color and keeping your locks in prime condition. Best Hair Color Ideas: 6 Fabulous Options to Consider We firmly believe that any color can work for any person. If you want bright pink hair with blue highlights in a pixie cut, go for it! But there are some guidelines to help you choose the best hair color idea for your complexion ⁠— let’s explain. Most hair colors either lean towards warm or cool tones. The same goes for your skin tone. If you have yellow, gold, or peachy undertones, you have a warm complexion. If you have blue or pink undertones, your complexion is cool. Not sure which one describes you? Here’s a quick trick: Examine the color of the veins on your wrist to determine the type of complexion you have. Blue veins mean you have cool undertones and green veins mean you have warm undertones. For your hair and skin tone to complement each other, select a hair color that’s within your warm or cool color family. Let’s review six on-trend hair color ideas to see which ones might work for you. Chocolate Brown Chocolate brown is one of the richest, most beautiful hair shades out there. It looks amazing on those with warm golden skin tones and can bring out any eye color. Since this is such a dimensional shade, we’d only suggest it for those with a lot of time to commit to the chocolatey aesthetic. If your natural hair color is much lighter or darker than chocolate, you’ll need frequent touch-ups to maintain this rich hue. Pro Tip: Check out more brown hair color ideas. Bronde There’s a fine line between dirty blonde and light brown hair and it’s called bronde. This color blends blonde and brown tones to give you a trendy, low-maintenance look. Being “bronde” can truly work for everybody, so long as you choose the right shade for you. If you have naturally dark hair and are looking to go bronde, we’d first recommend getting darker blonde highlights. Choosing golden blonde or caramel highlights will give you a bronde look you can easily maintain when your dark roots grow out. For blondes wanting to go darker, ask your colorist for lowlights in brunette shades like mushroom or light golden brown. Gray The gray hair color trend can look modern, playful, and sophisticated all at the same time. Gray shades work best on those with cool undertones. If you’re looking to layer a gray tone over your current color, choose a shade close to your natural hue. If you have naturally lighter hair, go with a light lavender or silvery blonde hue. If your hair is naturally dark, a charcoal or blue-gray shade will flatter your tresses. Pro Tip: Explore more gray hair color ideas. Black Give your hairstyle the ultimate edge by dying it the darkest shade of all. Black hair is undeniably mysterious and dramatic, especially if you’ve been rocking lighter tresses for some time. If you’re not sure if this raven-toned hair color idea is for you, here are some things to consider. Paler complexions with cool undertones will find black hair to be more flattering than those with peachy, warm undertones who may find that this dark shade washes them out. If you have a medium to darker skin tone, your richer pigment allows you to pull off this dramatic shade well. If your complexion is rich in golden or yellow undertones, mix in mocha brown balayage highlights to add multidimensional warm tones to your tresses. Rose Gold The pastel hair trend is still having a moment, but this time it’s veering into natural tones with redhead-adjacent shades of rose gold. This color looks kind of like strawberry blonde but has more pinky elements to it, making it best for those with warm, golden, or peach undertones. If you want to experiment with this cotton candy shade, layer a rose gold ombre hair color over your locks or add some peekaboo hair highlights to the ends of your tresses. Pro Tip: Got redhead curiosity? Check out more red hair color ideas. Platinum Blonde Platinum blonde is an iconic shade that many desire but few have the guts to commit to. If you love this Barbie-like blonde hair color idea but are afraid you can’t pull it off, think again. Platinum naturally complements those with pale skin and light eyes, but having these features isn’t required to rock this cool blonde shade. If your skin has cool undertones (and you’re ready for all the attention this color is going to give you), go platinum! The biggest question and concern about going platinum is whether bleaching it will destroy one’s hair. The answer is yes ⁠— unless you take the right steps to prevent major damage. The bleaching process is toughest on black or brunette hair because the darker your natural hair color is, the more rounds of bleach you’ll have to go through to get it to platinum. So if you’re dead set on taking your dark hair to the lightest of light shades, you have to commit to routine TLC for your tresses. Pro Tip: Try a purple shampoo to preserve platinum color and combat brassy tones. How to Care for Color-Treated Hair The downside of committing to a new hair color is that it can come with some degree of hair damage. Hair dye works by penetrating hair cuticles to deposit or remove color in the cortex, causing swelling and some damage to the hair strands. Regular dye jobs can cause your hair to feel rough, dry, tangled, and frizzy. Luckily, using a hair mask can make your hair look and feel a lot better. Function of Beauty’s customized hair mask is made to help replenish color damaged hair. It’s created with conditioning agents like argan oil, Japanese sake, and jojoba ester oil to give you more hydration than a traditional conditioner. Coat your strands with this product once or twice a week to improve softness and help restore the moisture your tresses need. Now That You’ve Found the Best Hair Color Idea ... With so many hair color ideas, it can be daunting to choose one. items.title: Damaged Hair: Causes, Signs, and 9 Ways to Prevent Further Damage
items.summary: Key Takeaways Hair damage occurs when the protective cuticle layer becomes compromised by heat, friction, chemical treatments, environmental exposure, or harsh grooming habits. Common signs of damaged hair include dryness, frizz, dullness, split ends, breakage, rough texture, and increased tangling. Gentle hair care habits, including careful detangling and reducing unnecessary friction, can help minimize future damage. Heat styling, chemical processing, chlorine, salt water, and excessive brushing can all contribute to weakening the hair fiber over time. Hydration is essential for maintaining healthy-looking hair and helping improve softness, smoothness, and manageability. Deep conditioning treatments, leave-in conditioners, and heat protectants can help support the hair's moisture balance and protective barrier.
